Q: node-mongo-native migration framework A:

I've just finished writing a basic migration framework based on node-mongo-native: https://github.com/afloyd/mongo-migrate. It will allow you to migrate up & down, as well as migrating up/down to a specific revision number. It was initially based on node-migrate, but obviously needed to be changed a bit to make it work.

The revision history is stored in mongodb and not on the file system like node-migrate, allowing collaboration on the same project using a single database. Otherwise each developer running migrations could cause migrations to run more than once against a database.

The migrations themselves are file-based, also helping with collaboration on a single project where each developer is (or is not) not using the same database. So when each dev runs the migration, all migration files not already run against his/her database will be run.

Check out the documentation for more info.

Q: SQL Basics: Create a FUNCTION (DATES) A:

Postgres has a built-in age() function that does that. You can just extract() the year part from it:
demo at db<>fiddle

create function agecalculator(date)
returns int return extract(years from age($1));

I don't see anything in the task that required you to use PL/pgSQL so I think you can just use a plain SQL function like this. I'm not sure why you tried to make it a set-returning/table function - the task asked for it to yield an int, so you should be fine with a scalar function.

As to why your version misbehaved, it's because when you subtract, then justify the interval, you lose track of leap years and interval length differences that result from the varying month lengths relative to the date of birth and the current date. The function justify_interval() assumes all months are exactly 30 days long and it doesn't account for leap years at all:
justify_days ( interval ) → interval
Adjust interval, converting 30-day time periods to months
justify_days(interval '1 year 65 days') → 1 year 2 mons 5 days
justify_hours ( interval ) → interval
Adjust interval, converting 24-hour time periods to days
justify_hours(interval '50 hours 10 minutes') → 2 days 02:10:00
justify_interval ( interval ) → interval
Adjust interval using justify_days and justify_hours, with additional sign adjustments
justify_interval(interval '1 mon -1 hour') → 29 days 23:00:00		 
select*,now()-age as raw_interval_subtraction
       ,JUSTIFY_INTERVAL(NOW() - age) as justified
       ,EXTRACT(YEAR FROM JUSTIFY_INTERVAL(NOW() - age)) as extracted
       ,age(age) as actual_age
from people
order by id
limit 3;
id name age raw_interval_subtraction justified extracted actual_age
1 Douglass Runolfsdottir 1975-05-24 18641 days 11:43:37.592109 51 years 9 mons 11 days 11:43:37.592109 51 51 years 13 days
2 Mr. Jc Donnelly 1992-11-15 12256 days 10:43:37.592109 34 years 16 days 10:43:37.592109 34 33 years 6 mons 21 days
3 Leta Rath I 1932-08-07 34271 days 11:43:37.592109 95 years 2 mons 11 days 11:43:37.592109 95 93 years 9 mons 30 days

Note that the raw subtraction result isn't wrong, it's just that the amount of days it showed translates to different lengths in years and months depending on what date you're measuring from. Not only does justify_interval() completely ignore that, it actually thinks a year is always 360 days long, because it assumes 12 months, 30 days each.

alter function agecalculator(date)rename to agecalculator_wrong;

create function agecalculator(date)
returns int return extract(years from age($1));

select*,agecalculator(age)
       ,agecalculator_wrong(age)
       ,abs(agecalculator_wrong(age)-agecalculator(age)) as mistake
from people
order by id
limit 3;
id name age agecalculator agecalculator_wrong mistake
1 Douglass Runolfsdottir 1975-05-24 51 51 0
2 Mr. Jc Donnelly 1992-11-15 33 34 1
3 Leta Rath I 1932-08-07 93 95 2

Q: AIX 7.1 to 7.2 migration experience with WebSphere Application Server 7.0.0.23 running on Java 6 A:

I'll just address IBM MQ related points. WebSphere MQ V7.5 is not supported on AIX 7.2. I'm not certain whether MQ V8 is because it's so old that the system pre-requisites information is no longer available on the IBM site!

When migrating to a newer version, you need to ensure that you can migrate from MQ V7.5 to the version you choose. There will be some versions that require a double jump. The newest version you can directly migrate to from MQ V7.5 is MQ V9.0. It is supported on AIX 7.2.

However, MQ V9.0 is no longer in support, so you would be advised to only use that as a stepping stone to get to a supported version, e.g. V9.4. You can go straight from V9.0 to any of the other V9.x versions.

You don't mention anything about what your MQ Queue Manager connects to on other machines? While any version connecting to any other version has long been a provision of MQ, there are other factors to consider such as whether there is any overlap with cipherspecs that can be used. If your other queue managers are also this old, and you upgrade this one to be very new, there will be very few choices.

  • Migration Paths (including from V7.5)

  • Migration Paths (including most recent versions)

Q: In C# 14 how to sort an array in reverse order? A:

The following doesn't matter in the specific case of integer arrays (because identical integers cannot be distinguished), but be aware than some of your candidate sorting methods are stable (i.e. they preserve the order of items that compare as equal) while others are not:

  • The Array.Sort() methods are documented to be unstable sorts:

    This implementation performs an unstable sort; that is, if two elements are equal, their order might not be preserved. In contrast, a stable sort preserves the order of elements that are equal.

  • The Enumerable ordering methods are stable. E.g. from the Enumerable.OrderByDescending() docs:

    This method performs a stable sort; that is, if the keys of two elements are equal, the order of the elements is preserved. In contrast, an unstable sort does not preserve the order of elements that have the same key.

  • The stability of the MemoryExtensions.Sort() seems to be undocumented as of .NET 10.

  • arr.Sort(); is actually arr.AsSpan().Sort() so its stability is also undocumented.

If you are sorting arrays where duplicate comparisons may occur for non-identical items (e.g. you are sorting an array of records by price where different objects may have the same price) then all these sort-and-reverse algorithms may produce different results. Before optimizing for code style or performance, I'd recommend to make sure you don't need to care about sort stability.

If you know you don't care about stability, you should benchmark yourself to find the most performant for your particular objects. (See Eric Lippert's rant Which is faster?) And if performance is comparable my recommendation would be to do things in one line of code.

To create a new, sorted array, do:

var sortedArr = arr.OrderDescending().ToArray();

To sort in place, do:

arr.Sort((x, y) => y.CompareTo(x));
